newsitem.title: INDIA: Cautious outlook for Indian stocks in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Cautious outlook for Indian stocks in 1997.

text.p: Indian stock markets are heading into the New Year with hopes for a respite from the severe bear run of the past two years but the path ahead is pitted with fundamental weaknesses, analysts warned.

Lingering problems include political uncertainties, sluggish industrial growth, slowing demand and fears of increases in government-fixed oil prices which would trigger higher freight and energy costs, they said.
"I see a period of constraints on the macro-front," said R. Balakrishnan, president of Dil Vikas Finance Ltd, a broking firm at the National Stock Exchange.
He said infrastructural bottlenecks and other constraints would hit company earnings in 1996/97 (April-March).
"The markets will be led by valuations (because of the slump in share prices) rather than by earnings growth," he said.
"It is a stay-away market. Indian markets have been a losing story since September 1994."
The top-30 share index of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) hit an intraday record high of 4,643.31 on September 12, 1994, but has since been on a prolonged downtrend.
On December 4 this year, the index plunged to a three-year low of 2,713.12 against the year's high of 4,131.22 reached on June 17.
A late rally helped the benchmark index finish 1996 at 3,085.20, down 25.29 points, or 0.81 percent, from the close of 1995. The Bombay bourse, on holiday since December 25, reopens on January 1.
Some analysts were not impressed by the surge.

"We believe it is a bear market rally built on a lot of hope and anticipation and will fizzle out in the New Year when confronted with disappointing news," said analyst Praween Napate at broking and securities firm ING Barings.
"We continue to recommend restructuring portfolios and exit from auto, cement, steel," he said in a report.
But Sanjeev Choithani, chief dealer at broker Pashupati Advani, said he was confident of a turnaround.
"The market has bottomed out. It's in a consolidation phase before it moves up," he said. "I see growth of 20 percent (in the BSE index) in 1997."

Brokerage Asit C. Mehta Investment Intermediates Ltd said the late surge was due to foreign fund buying to boost the net asset value (NAV) of their exposures which is calculated on the basis of closing prices for the year.
"Whether these NAVs reflect NRVs (net realisable values) is a matter of conjecture," it said in a report.
The firm expects the market to stay bullish in the run-up to the annual government budget due in late February for the fiscal year 1997/98 (April-March).
Analysts saw a silver lining in stronger farm output which would boost rural incomes, and the possibility of lower interest rates.
"Prospects are brightening," said Anindya Chatterjee, economic analyst at Natwest Markets. "Falling real interest rates and stronger rural demand will stimulate consumption and investment."

The Reserve Bank of India, the central bank, has announced it will cut the cash reserve ratio (CRR) of banks by 0.5 percentage point twice in January, on January 4 and January 18. The move will release 42.75 billion rupees ($1.19 billion) into the banking system.
Chatterjee expects the cuts will bring down bank interest rates.
Several state-run banks reduced their prime lending rates by 0.5-1.0 percentage points to 14.5-15.0 percent a year, following similar CRR cuts in October and November.
Analysts also said the slump in world commodities prices was one factor that accelerated the bearish phase on Indian bourses.
"The key to 1997 depends on how quickly the commodities cycle bottoms out," Dil Vikas' Balakrishnan said.
Falling world prices hit Indian firms' export margins and also posed the threat of cheaper imports.
